data.title: Discovery — does the pain that `kadence decision` is meant to cure exist
body: # Discovery — does the pain that `kadence decision` is meant to cure exist
- **Method:** desk research (Tavily), 2 queries + reading two sources in full
- **The decision it supports:** whether `kadence decision` stays in Next, and what exactly to ask about it in Probe B
- **Labels:** **Fact** — said by the primary source · **Finding** — our reading · **Assumption** — without proof
## Why this research

The [roadmap](DOC-33) puts `kadence decision` in Next with one dependency: Probe B has to show that people **already** try to capture "why". If they do not try, we are offering discipline, not a tool.

Probe B cannot be run without people. But the question "does this pain exist outside our own head" is partly checkable at the desk, and the answer changes **what exactly** to ask in the conversations.
## Finding 1 — the pain is named, and named in someone else's words

A practitioner working with Claude Code and Codex describes the mechanics of the loss directly: **what** was done survives context compaction, **why** it was done that way does not. The consequence is stated without our involvement: the next instance of the agent proposes the rejected approach again, because it does not know it was rejected — **Fact** ([Compaction Memory](https://gist.github.com/sigalovskinick/e2e329bb37ecc74b9f15d5ba74ee1ee5)).

The record format he proposes — `Decision: X. Why: Y. Rejected: Z.` — **Fact**, same source. This is almost word for word the shape of the event we planned for `kadence decision`, invented independently and under the pressure of real work.
He also calls it the second most impactful rule in his set, and in the "minimal 5-minute setup" he keeps exactly two rules out of eight — and this is one of them — **Fact**.

**What this changes.** The `kadence decision` bet stops being pure guesswork. The problem it cures is described by a person who does not know we exist, in terms closer to ours than anything found earlier — **Finding**, high confidence.
## Finding 2 — ADRs are coming back precisely because of agents

The practice of architecture decision records, which teams quietly abandoned at the end of the 2010s, is described as having come back and become load-bearing for teams where an agent touches production — **Fact** ([The ADR Comeback](https://rickpollick.com/blog/adr-comeback-anchoring-agentic-engineering-teams)).
Same source: in the ADR template, the section **"Alternatives considered"** is named as the one that pays for itself. The record's status takes the value `Superseded by ADR-NNN` — **Fact**.

**What this changes.** The category is not empty, and it is moving in our direction. But it is moving towards **documents**, not towards events, and that is a difference to be defended with an argument rather than sidestepped — **Finding**.
## Finding 3 — why ADRs used to die

Three reasons, named by several sources independently — **Fact** ([hidekazu-konishi](https://hidekazu-konishi.com/entry/architecture_decision_records_templates_and_operations.html), [neilsherman](https://www.neilsherman.co.uk/blog/architecture-decision-records.html)):
1. **The records became ceremony.** They were written after the decision had already shipped — ratification instead of capture. Engineers rightly noticed that the effort yielded no information.

2. **The format was chosen, the operating model was not.** Nobody decided **when** a record is mandatory, who reads it and where it sits in the daily flow. The practice turns into "write it if you remember", which means it does not get written.
3. **A single author.** When he leaves, the practice ends.

**What this changes — the most in the whole document.** These are not arguments against `kadence decision`; they are the specification for it. A team can adopt the tool and still never start using it if we do not answer "when is this mandatory" — **Finding**.

Our advantage here is structural: the event is written **at the moment of the action**, through the same command that moves the task, not as a separate ritual afterwards. Reason No. 1 (ceremony) is architecturally made harder. Reasons No. 2 and No. 3 are not, and nothing saves us from them — **Finding**.
## Finding 4 — the counter-evidence that has to be designed inwards

A rejected option does not stay wrong forever: the library gets fixed, the limitation disappears — and the agent quotes the old rationale as current — **Fact** (a practitioner's comment, [r/ClaudeAI](https://www.reddit.com/r/ClaudeAI/comments/1w3j7tl/my_coding_agent_keeps_reproposing_the_thing_we)).
For an append-only journal this is a direct challenge: we do not edit events. ADRs solve it with the `Superseded by` status.

**What this changes.** `kadence decision` cannot simply be an event type with text. It needs a **superseding** mechanism — a new event that marks the old one as no longer current, and a fold that hands the agent the current set of decisions rather than every one ever recorded. Otherwise we will build a machine for quoting outdated reasons — **Finding**, high confidence.
This agrees with an existing invariant: we already do this for task statuses. Nothing new is needed in the data model — what is needed is a deliberate design of the fold.
## Finding 5 — an adjacent competitor that is not in our snapshot

`mem0` is a memory layer for agents that stores decisions with metadata and timestamps, with an explicit item "remembers what we already tried and rejected"; **62,590 stars** at the time of checking — **Fact** ([mem0](https://mem0.ai/blog/ai-coding-agents-that-actually-remember-your-codebase)).

It is not a task tracker, so the [competitive snapshot](DOC-41) did not see it. But it promises **the same outcome** as our bet on shared context, by a different mechanism: an external service instead of files in the repository.

**What this changes.** The comparison of "who has the better journal" is incomplete. The real alternative for a user is not Backlog.md but "install a memory layer and stop thinking about files". Our arguments against: offline, zero services, the data lives on the branch together with the code. Whether these arguments are enough is an **Assumption**, and it is exactly the one now worth a question in Probe B — **Finding**.
## What this changes in the roadmap
| Was | Became |

| `kadence decision` — the gate: whether the pain exists | The pain is **described from outside**. The gate shifts: not "does it exist" but **"is our mechanism better than the workarounds already in use"** |
| Probe B asks whether people capture "why" | Probe B has to ask **where they do it now** — compaction prompts, ADRs, mem0, Slack, their head — and what is wrong with it |
| The `decision` event — text with a reason | **Superseding** is needed: decisions go stale, and an agent quoting a reversed reason is worse than an agent with no memory |
## What this research did not answer

How many teams feel this is not known. All the findings come from practitioners who are **already** deep in agent work and were already looking for a solution; this is the most biased sample possible. They prove that the pain exists, and say nothing about how widespread it is — that it is typical is an **Assumption**.

And the main thing: no source says that people want a **task tracker** that can do this. They describe the agent's memory problem, and the solutions they reach for are prompts and memory services, not a journal of the work in the repository. Whether these two needs are one, or two adjacent ones, desk research does not settle. That is exactly what Probe B exists for.
## Addendum 2026-09-08 — how others do it
### Backlog.md has already shipped it

Our nearest competitor has **both** commands we planned: `backlog doc` and `backlog decision`. The directory structure is `backlog/{tasks,drafts,docs,decisions,archive,completed}`, everything as Markdown with YAML front matter; `backlog search` does a fuzzy search **across tasks, documents and decisions together** — **Fact** ([the repository](https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md), [a review with `--help` output](https://en.thedavestack.com/backlog-md)).

There is even a third-party Claude Code skill that manages their tasks, specifications and ADRs through their CLI — **Fact** ([MCP Market](https://mcpmarket.com/tools/skills/backlog-md-task-decision-manager)).
**We are not first and will not be.** This does not stop the work, but it changes the argument: the differentiation cannot be "we have decisions", because they have them too.
### What is established in ADR tools

- Each record is a separate file with monotonic numbering; status `proposed` → `accepted` → `superseded` / `deprecated`. **An accepted ADR is never rewritten — it is superseded**, so that a journal remains of how long the decision was in force — **Fact** ([Fowler](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ArchitectureDecisionRecord.html)).

- log4brains states it plainly: an ADR is immutable, only the status can change, and thanks to that the documentation never goes stale — **Fact** ([log4brains](https://github.com/thomvaill/log4brains)).

- `adr-tools` can do `adr new -s3 "…"` — it creates a new record **and** sets `Superseded by` on the old one, that is, a link in both directions — **Fact** ([hascode](https://www.hascode.com/managing-architecture-decision-records-with-adr-tools)).
- The ecosystem is large: adr-tools and a dozen rewrites in different languages, log4brains, MADR tooling, a Backstage plugin — **Fact** ([adr.github.io](https://adr.github.io/adr-tooling)).

**The most important thing:** the ADR philosophy is **append-only with superseding**. That is the same thing our core already does. We are not bringing someone else's idea into the event model; we found that the event model is the native form for a practice others implement with files.
### Two cracks everyone has and nobody has closed

**Crack 1 — superseding is updated on one side.** The source states it plainly: most teams update one side and forget the other, **and that is exactly how a reversed decision keeps looking current** — **Fact** ([Scribelet](https://scribelet.app/blog/architecture-decision-record-examples)).

This is exactly the failure we anticipated in the [roadmap](DOC-33) from the other side — an agent quoting a reversed reason. It is now confirmed as a **mass disease of the existing tools**, not as our hypothetical risk.

For a file-based tool this is inevitable: superseding is two edits in two files, and the second one may not happen. **In an event journal, superseding is one event**, and both directions are derived while folding. It cannot half-apply — **Finding**, and this is the hardest structural argument we have.

**Crack 2 — the numbering conflicts in git.** log4brains deliberately **dropped numbering in the files**, and the reason is named plainly: to avoid merge problems in git — **Fact** ([log4brains](https://github.com/thomvaill/log4brains)).

That is, a mature ADR implementation ran into exactly the problem [Probe A](DOC-55) measured, and paid for it with the loss of readable numbers. For us the ULID is primary and `KAD-N` is derived while folding (invariant I7) — we have both conflict-freedom and numbers — **Finding**.

**Crack 3, which nobody has closed:** all the tools can create and number, and **none of them notices when an accepted decision has stopped matching the code** — **Fact** ([Scribelet](https://scribelet.app/blog/architecture-decision-record-examples)). This is an open problem of the industry, not our niche for tomorrow.
### What this changes
| | Was | Became |
| The argument | "we will have decisions" | does not work — Backlog.md already has them |

| Differentiation | not formulated | **atomic superseding** and **numbers without conflicts** — both structural, both following from the event model, both confirmed as real pains of other people's tools |
| The risk | that the pain is invented | that the pain is real but **rarely felt** — the same trap as with conflict-free merging |
